claim: Constrained decoding that only keeps each prefix extendable to some valid string can still fail to finish a valid output within a finite token budget, especially when the model's subword tokens do not line up with the grammar's terminals; precomputing, for a bounded-stack summary of the grammar's pushdown automaton, an upper bound on how many tokens are still needed to reach acceptance, and pruning any continuation whose bound exceeds the remaining budget, guarantees that every returned output is grammatical. Supported only if, with a 120-token budget, the decoder produces 100% syntactically valid outputs on JSON, SQL and linear temporal logic for all three base models tested and 100% schema-valid JSON, while every prefix-masking decoder (Guidance, Outlines, XGrammar, SynCode) and sequential Monte Carlo steering stay below 100% schema validity on every model even with budgets raised to 4,096 tokens; and if its JSON decoding is faster than sampling ten outputs and filtering for validity.

experiments: Define the decoder. Setup: translate the grammar to a pushdown automaton; offline, compute bounded-stack summaries (stack height H) with Pre*-style reachability and, by weighting each terminal with the minimum number of model tokens needed to emit it, an upper bound on the token distance to acceptance. Online, track configurations including a partially matched terminal so subword tokens can cross terminal boundaries; combine the model's top-k tokens with automaton-proposed tokens, keep only those whose successors can still reach acceptance within the remaining budget, push the logits of tokens that make progress towards acceptance toward the best viable logit (strength alpha), and run beam search; configurations missing from the cache are computed on the fly. A theorem shows every returned output is accepted and one is returned whenever the bound fits the budget. Preprocessing takes 0.29 s for schema-specific JSON grammars, 0.42 s for LTL (H = 50) and 3 h 40 min for SQL (H = 13).

Fix the benchmarks and baselines. Setup: Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, Llama-3.2-3B-Instruct and Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct; json-mode-eval (100 schema-conditioned JSON examples), Spider validation (1,034 text-to-SQL), and the drone-planning LTL golden set (6,185); token budget 120 for all. Baselines: the unconstrained model (temperature 0.8, 10 seeds), sample-and-verify over those 10 samples, Guidance, Outlines, XGrammar, SynCode (strict) and GenLM sequential Monte Carlo (2 or 5 particles) where their public code supports the grammar; XGrammar dropped for SQL at about 20 s per token; no baseline supports LTL natively except SynCode. Metrics: syntactic validity, JSON schema validity, SQL execution accuracy, LTL accuracy by Buchi-automaton equivalence, perplexity under the base model, and seconds per output.

Generate JSON. Result: syntactic / schema validity 100 / 100% on all three models, against at best 96 / 90% (Llama-3.1-8B; Guidance and Outlines), 95 / 90% (Llama-3.2-3B; XGrammar, Outlines) and 96 / 89% (Qwen2.5-7B; sample-and-verify, Outlines, GenLM); unconstrained 63.7 / 57.1, 56.4 / 49.4 and 93.6 / 87.4%. Time 3.46-4.05 s per output, against 9.65-17.38 s for sample-and-verify and 0.96-3.62 s for masking decoders; perplexity 1.11-1.14 against 1.01-1.08 for most baselines and 1.38-1.80 for XGrammar.

Check whether local decoders just need more tokens. Setup: rerun JSON with budgets 512, 1,024, 2,048 and 4,096 for Guidance, Outlines, SynCode and GenLM. Result: syntactic validity reaches 95-100% but schema validity stays at 79-93% for every method and model, essentially flat across budgets (e.g. SynCode 83% on Llama-3.1-8B at every budget while its time grows from 13.27 to 113.81 s); the authors attribute this to local decoders opening nested structures without a signal to close them.

Note what makes JSON schema validity attainable. Setup: the decoder is given a grammar compiled from each example's schema, so grammatical acceptance implies schema validity, whereas baselines use their own schema support; deterministic decoders are reported from a single run; the sample-and-verify baseline draws only 10 samples per input. The guarantee also holds only when the bounded summary certifies a completion within the budget; otherwise the decoder reports failure instead of an output.
